figure.caption: The secant line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(a + h, f(a + h))$ has slope $\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$. As $h \to 0$ it turns into the tangent line at $x = a$, whose slope is $f'(a)$.

chain.effect: its value is called the derivative of $f$ at $a$, written $f'(a)$

chain.cause: Secant lines through $(a, f(a))$ pivot as $h \to 0$
chain.effect: they approach the tangent line at $x = a$, whose slope is $f'(a)$

chain.cause: The derivative is found at every input where the limit exists
chain.effect: the result is a new function, $f'(x)$, also written $y'$ or $\frac{dy}{dx}$
the tangent line is $y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$

ideas: The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is $f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$, or equivalently $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$. Both are the same limit of secant slopes.
The tangent line at $x = a$ passes through $(a, f(a))$ with slope $f'(a)$: $y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$.
Done at every $x$, the limit gives the derivative function $f'(x)$. In Leibniz notation, $y = f(x)$ has derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$, and $\frac{d}{dx}$ means "the derivative of".
A derivative has the units of a rate: output units per input unit.

misconception.wrong: $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(3 + h)^2 - 9}{h}$ is a strange limit to evaluate by plugging in, so it is $\frac{0}{0}$ and undefined.
misconception.right: Read its shape. It is $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(3 + h) - f(3)}{h}$ with $f(x) = x^2$, so it is $f'(3)$, the slope of $y = x^2$ at $x = 3$. Simplify and it equals 6. A limit of a difference quotient is a derivative at a point.

summary: The derivative $f'(a)$ is the limit of the difference quotient as $h \to 0$: the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $a$ and the slope of the tangent line there. Found at every $x$, it is the function $f'(x) = \frac{dy}{dx}$. The tangent line at $a$ is $y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$.
